thread.title_full: Ducks Unlimited partners with Groundswell for Rock County conservation project - NewsBreak

author: TIM SULLIVAN
title: Ducks Unlimited partners with Groundswell for Rock County conservation project - NewsBreak
text:
By TIM SULLIVAN ALEX GARY ,
16 hours ago
TOWN OF AVON — More details have emerged from Ducks Unlimited’s $4.7 million acquisition of 20.26 acres in the Town of Avon to turn farmland into a protected wetland area.
Ducks Unlimited is partnering with Groundswell, a conservation-oriented nonprofit organization, to ensure public access to the green space adjacent to the Avon Bottoms Wildlife Area and State Natural Area.
“As a local land trust, we’re grateful for the opportunity to partner with an international organization in Ducks Unlimited to protect this very significant resource for southern Wisconsin,” said Groundswell Executive Director Heidi Habeger.
Groundswell, based in Madison, operates in several counties in south central Wisconsin, with a focus on Dane and its adjacent counties.
On June 29, the county recorded the sale from Applegate-Bader Farm LLC of Monroe to the Wetlands America Trust Inc. of Dexter, Mich. According to its website, Wetlands America Trust is one of the largest accredited land trusts in the United States, holding conservation easements on more than 500,000 acres.
Wetlands America Trust is the official land trust and supporting foundation for Tennessee-based Ducks Unlimited. Ducks Unlimited, which was founded in 1937 during the Dust Bowl, is the world’s largest nonprofit organization dedicated to the conservation of wetlands and upland habitats. In Wisconsin alone, the organization owns and conserves more than 134,000 acres.
“This project demonstrates what is possible when conservation organizations, generous landowners, donors, and public partners unite behind a shared vision,” said Ducks Unlimited Upper Midwest Director of Conservation Programs Brian Glenzinski. “By protecting this remarkable landscape, we’re conserving vital wildlife habitat, improving water quality and flood resilience, and ensuring future generations can enjoy Wisconsin’s rich outdoor traditions.”
Applegate-Bader Farm LLC of Monroe is interesting in its own right. Applegate-Bader operates a large-scale 11,000-acre agricultural operation in Green County, with about 2,000 acres enrolled in the federal Wetland Reserve Easement program.
Applegate-Bader Farm also was the plaintiff in a couple of high-profile legal cases against the State of Wisconsin. Hoping to lower its property taxes, the farming entity sued the Wisconsin Department of Revenue in 2016 questioning whether agency actions and economic impact statements were properly evaluated and also challenged the state’s decision not to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) under the Wisconsin Environmental Policy Act in connection with a local transmission line.
In 2021, the Wisconsin State Supreme Court ruled in favor of Applegate-Bader on the environmental impact statement issue, ruling that the Department of Revenue failed to adequately document its rationale for not preparing an EIS. But the court ruled in favor of the Department of Revenue on the evaluation issue, ruling that the state did not fail in its economic impact analyses.
The Ducks Unlimited deal was the 10th so far in Rock County in 2026 where more than $1 million was spent on farmland. The next biggest price tag also was in June when Evansville Land Holdings LLC paid $2.34 million for 175 acres in the Town of Magnolia at 4724 N. Coon Island Rd.
The Knowles-Nelson Stewardship program provided a grant to assist in the acquisition of the property. The program was named after former governors Warren Knowles and Gaylord Nelson. Run through the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, Knowles-Nelson was tasked with providing opportunities for conservation organizations and the DNR itself to purchase or maintain land intended for outdoor recreation for Wisconsinites.
“Acquiring this property is a huge win for wildlife and outdoor recreation,” said DNR wildlife biologist Jason Cotter, who manages the Avon Bottoms Wildlife Area. “Public access lands are limited in this part of the state, despite nearly 2 million people living within an hour’s drive. This achievement was only possible because of strong partnerships and a shared commitment to protecting these natural resources.”
First passed under Governor Tommy Thompson in 1989, Knowles-Nelson was not funded in the most recent state budget, and its authorization lapsed June 30, making this project one of the last to benefit from its initial existence. The program can be reauthorized in a new legislative session.
Other funding for the acquisition project was contributed by a North American Wetlands Conservation Act grant through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and several private donors. Other support was provided by conservation partners including the National Wild Turkey Federation and Pheasants Forever.
